Learning Objectives
Discuss standard shoulder radiographs that should be obtained for all patients being
evaluated for shoulder arthritis.
Identify etiologies of primary osteoarthritis and discuss the utility of radiographs in identifying
the underlying etiology.
Explain when advanced imaging studies should be obtained in patients in whom shoulder
arthritis is suspected.
Review common classification schemes for primary glenohumeral arthritis.
Review common classification schemes for rotator cuff arthropathy.
Review common classification schemes for osteonecrosis of the humeral head.

Identify secondary causes of shoulder arthritis that should be considered in evaluating
shoulder imaging studies.
Imaging Modalities
Radiographs should be obtained for all patients to identify the etiology of shoulder arthritis.
The need for advanced imaging studies can be determined after reviewing plain radiographs.
CT is the preferred imaging modality for additional evaluation of glenoid morphology.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality to assess soft-tissue structures, including the rotator
cuff.

Imaging Modalities
Glenohumeral arthritis is characterized by damage to the articular surfaces of the
humeral head and/or glenoid. Many etiologies can contribute to degeneration of the
glenohumeral joint, from primary osteoarthritis to secondary causes of joint
degeneration (ie, rotator cuff arthropathy, osteonecrosis of the humeral head,
posttraumatic arthritis, dislocation arthropathy, postcapsulorrhaphy, inflammatory
arthropathy, or chondrolysis).1 Identifying the etiology and severity of joint degeneration
plays an integral role in identifying possible treatment options for patients (Videos 1 and
2).

Radiographs should be obtained for all patients being evaluated for glenohumeral
arthritis. Recommended views include a true AP view of the glenohumeral joint, an AP
view, and an axillary lateral view. Important considerations in interpreting radiographs
include evaluating the effective joint space and cartilage thickness; evaluating the
cephalad-caudal relationship of the humerus to the glenoid; assessing the
acromiohumeral interval (AHI); and evaluating for morphologic changes to the humerus
and glenoid, including glenoid wear patterns and glenoid version. These radiographic
findings often help identify the etiology of degenerative findings and help determine the
need for advanced imaging studies for preoperative planning purposes.
Glenohumeral arthritis may substantially alter glenoid morphology, and CT scans should
be obtained for further definition of abnormal glenoid morphology. Common pathologic
changes include posterior wear of the glenoid and posterior humeral head subluxation
in the setting of osteoarthritis.2 In addition, pathologic changes to the glenoid may result
in changes to glenoid version. Failure to identify these pathologic changes before
shoulder arthroplasty may lead to suboptimal restoration of normal biomechanics,
which may increase the risk for premature glenoid component loosening and recurrent
subluxation of the humeral head. CT scans are the preferred imaging study for
evaluating glenoid version and bone stock. Preoperative planning software often uses CT
data, particularly for difficult glenoid reconstruction. CT scans also may provide some
information on rotator cuff pathology; however, CT scans may underestimate full-
thickness rotator cuff tears, fatty infiltration, and muscle atrophy compared with MRIs.3
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for assessing soft-tissue structures and should be
considered if concern exists for rotator cuff pathology that is not clearly defined via
clinical examination or CT scans. MRI is not as accurate as CT in assessing bony glenoid
morphology and is less accurate in the classification of highly degenerative glenoids.4
Primary Osteoarthritis
Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Articular cartilage loss and joint space loss with no known etiology

Characterized by the findings of joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral
cysts, and osteophytes (particularly along the inferior margin of the humeral head)

Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Primary osteoarthritis is characterized by radiographic degeneration of the glenoid and
the humeral head with no history of prior trauma or secondary causes of joint
degeneration. The classic findings of osteoarthritis are joint space narrowing, osteophyte
formation, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts (Figures 1 and 2). Morphologic
changes of the proximal humerus and the glenoid may occur as the disease progresses.
Most commonly, this includes posterior wear of the glenoid and posterior subluxation of
the humeral head. These changes can be identified on axillary radiographs and can be
further evaluated via CT to better characterize glenoid morphology, glenoid version, and
humeral head subluxation.
Figure 1 AP radiograph of the a shoulder demonstrates osteoarthritis of the
glenohumeral joint. Note the characteristic signs of osteoarthritis, including joint space
narrowing, osteophyte formation (white arrow), and subchondral sclerosis (black arrow).
(Reproduced from Blaine T: Osteoarthritis of the shoulder, in Johnson TR, Steinbach LS,
eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Imaging. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2003, pp 214-217.)

Classification Systems
Several classification schemes have been described for glenohumeral arthritis.
The Samilson-Prieto classification system is based on traditional findings observed in patients
with glenohumeral osteoarthritis.
The Walch classification system defines glenoid morphology and the position of the humeral
head relative to the glenoid and has important implications with regard to management.
Samilson-Prieto Cassification System

Samilson-Prieto Cassification System
The Samilson-Prieto classification system is a frequently cited classification scheme that
highlights the most common degenerative findings of glenohumeral arthritis.5 This
classification system has three grades: mild, moderate, and severe. Mild arthritis is
defined as inferior osteophytes smaller than 3 mm in size on the humeral head or the
glenoid. Moderate arthritis is associated with osteophyte complexes between 3 and 7

mm in height, with mild glenohumeral joint morphologic abnormalities. Severe arthritis
is associated with osteophyte complexes exceeding 7 mm in height, with narrowing of
the glenohumeral joint and sclerosis. Notably, this classification system is not associated
with the same degree of corresponding treatment implications as those associated with
the Walch classification system.
Walch Classification System

Walch Classification System
The Walch classification system is the most widely used classification scheme for glenoid
morphology6,7 (Resources 1 and 2). It accounts for glenoid wear patterns, glenoid
version, and the position of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. Walch et al6
recognized the importance of these variables with respect to total shoulder arthroplasty
outcomes and created a classification system that accounts for various patterns of
glenoid wear, abnormalities in glenoid version, and potential subluxation of the humeral
head. The classification system provides a framework for understanding the various
manners in which osteoarthritis may affect the glenohumeral joint and helps surgeons in
preoperative planning and surgical management.
Initially described in 1999, the Walch classification system was defined using axial
imaging from two-dimensional CT scans. Walch et al6 defined the glenoid wear pattern
as one of three main subtypes (Figure 3).

Figure 3 Illustrations show the Walch classification of glenoid morphology, which is
based on wear patterns and version. A, Type A1, centered humeral head with minor
glenoid erosion. B, Type A2, centered humeral head with major glenoid erosion. C, Type
B1, posterior subluxation with no erosion. D, Type B2, posterior erosion with a biconcave
glenoid. E, Type C, severe retroversion. (Reproduced from Sears BW, Johnston PS,
Ramsey ML, Williams GR: Glenoid bone loss in primary total shoulder arthroplasty:
Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[9]:604-613.)
Type A is characterized by a symmetric, concentric wear pattern of the glenoid with less
than 5% humeral head subluxation in the anterior or posterior direction. Type A is
subclassified into type A1 with minimal glenoid wear and type A2 with severe glenoid
wear and deeper central erosions.
Type B is characterized by asymmetric arthritis with posterior subluxation of the
humeral head. Type B is subclassified into type B1 with posterior subluxation of the
humeral head, posterior joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis
and type B2 with similar posterior subluxation of the humeral head in addition to
erosion of the posterior glenoid, resulting in biconcavity.
Type C represents a dysplastic type of glenoid that has retroversion greater than 25°
regardless of the glenoid erosion pattern or the location of the humeral head with
respect to the glenoid, suggesting the retroverted glenoid was present before arthritis
development.

In 2016, Bercik et al8 used three-dimensional CT scans to further modify the Walch
classification system to include type B3 and type D (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustrations show the modified Walch classification of glenoid morphology in
glenohumeral osteoarthritis. (Reproduced with permission from Bercik MJ, Kruse K II,
Yalizis M, Gauci MO, Chaoui J, Walch G: A modification to the Walch classification of the
glenoid in primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis using three-dimensional imaging. J
Shoulder Elbow Surg 2016;25[10]:1601-1606.)
Type B3 is a monoconcave-appearing glenoid with posterior wear and at least 15° of
retroversion and/or a minimum of 70% posterior humeral head subluxation.
Type D is a glenoid that has any degree of anteversion or anterior humeral head
subluxation.9
The definition of type A2 was refined and described to include a line connecting the
anterior and posterior rims of the glenoid that transects the humeral head (Resource 3).
Secondary Arthritis: Rotator Cuff Arthropathy
Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings

Joint degeneration that is a result of rotator cuff insufficiency
Characterized by radiographic findings of superior migration of the humeral head with
acetabularization of the acromion and femoralization of the humeral head

Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Rotator cuff arthropathy is associated with a specific pattern of joint degeneration that
results from a combination of rotator cuff insufficiency and resultant loss of joint
congruence and abnormal glenohumeral wear. Rotator cuff insufficiency alters joint
biomechanics such that a loss of the compression effect that the rotator cuff has on the
humeral head occurs, which results in superior migration of the humeral head with a
corresponding decrease in the AHI. This proximal migration of the humeral head
decentralizes the center of rotation, the amount of which depends on the extent of
rotator cuff tearing, integrity of the coracoacromial arch, and location of glenoid wear
and bone loss. The humeral head may eventually collapse as it migrates superiorly.
A standard series of shoulder radiographs should be obtained, including a true AP view,
AP view, and axillary lateral view. Classic radiographic findings include acetabularization
of the acromion, femoralization of the humeral head, an asymmetric superior wear
pattern of the glenoid, absence of osteophytes, and anterosuperior escape of the
humeral head. MRI typically is not necessary for evaluation of the rotator cuff,
particularly in patients with advanced stages of the disease because the level of rotator
cuff disease is such that a massive irreparable tear with retraction and associated fatty
infiltration/muscle atrophy is present. CT scans may be obtained for additional
assessment of glenoid morphology, to determine the extent of erosion into the
coracoacromial arch, and to determine the amount of available bone stock.
Classification Schemes
Several radiographic classification schemes have been developed to define the bony changes
observed in patients with rotator cuff tear arthropathy.
The Seebauer classification system targets the degree of superior migration from the center of
rotation and the amount of instability of the center of rotation.

The Hamada classification system defines the structural changes observed in the
coracoacromial arch.
Seebauer Classification System

Seebauer Classification System
The Seebauer classification system was designed based on biomechanical factors
associated with rotator cuff tear arthropathy and associated clinical outcomes from
shoulder arthroplasty10 (Resource 4). Four types are described, which are distinguished
based on the amount of superior migration from the center of rotation and the level of
instability of the resultant center of rotation (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Table shows the Seebauer classification of rotator cuff arthropathy.
(Reproduced with permission from Visotsky JL, Basamania C, Seebauer L, Rockwood CA,
Jensen KL: Cuff tear arthropathy: pathogenesis, classification, and algorithm for
treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2004;86[suppl 2]:35-40.)
Type I is characterized by a maintained center of rotation with intact anterior restraints
and minimal superior humeral head migration. Further subclassification includes type IA,
which is characterized as dynamic joint stabilization with femoralization of the humeral
head and acetabularization of the coracoacromial arch. Type IB is characterized by
additional medial erosion of the glenoid with resultant medialization of the center of
rotation and compromised dynamic joint stabilization in addition to the humeral head
femoralization and coracoacromial arch acetabularization observed in type IA.
Type II is characterized by a decentralized center of rotation from proximal migration of
the humeral head. Type IIA is characterized by limited stability from compromised
anterior restraints with superior translation, loss of dynamic joint stabilization, and
minimum stability provided by the coracoacromial arch. Type IIA is characterized by
superomedial erosion of the glenoid in addition to severe femoralization of the humeral
head and acetabularization of the coracoacromial arch.
Type IIB is characterized by a decentralized center of rotation and is considered
unstable. Anterosuperior escape from incompetent anterior structures and absence of
dynamic joint stabilization are noted.
Hamada Classification System

Hamada Classification System
The Hamada classification system was described in 1990 and characterizes the structural
changes within the coracoacromial arch in patients with rotator cuff tear arthropathy11-
13 (Resources 5, 6, and 7). The intent of the Hamada classification system is to account
for the progression of radiographic findings observed in patients with the disease.

Pathologic changes begin with deltoid contraction during forward elevation, which
results in superior migration of the humeral head and a decrease in the AHI.
Grade 1 is defined by an AHI of more than 6 mm.
Grade 2 is defined by an AHI of 5 mm or less.
Grade 3 is defined by an AHI of 5 mm or less, the presence of acromial acetabularization, and
a concave deformity on the undersurface of the acromion from the proximally migrated
humeral head abutting the acromion.
Grade 4 is characterized by narrowing of the glenohumeral joint in addition to grade 3
findings.
Grade 5 is characterized by humeral head collapse and is termed cuff tear arthropathy.
Walch et al6 identified subgroups of patients with a decreased AHI who did not have acromial
acetabularization, as is observed in grade 3; therefore, grade 4 was subdivided into grade 4A
and grade 4B.
Grade 4A is characterized by glenohumeral arthritis with an AHI of less than 7 mm and no
acromial acetabularization.
Grade 4B is characterized by glenohumeral arthritis with an AHI of 5 mm or less with acromial
acetabularization.
Secondary Arthritis: Osteonecrosis of the Humeral Head
Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Humeral head osteonecrosis is caused by an interruption in blood supply to the humeral head.
Classic radiographic findings include osteolytic lesions, subchondral sclerosis and collapse,
crescent signs, and depression of the articular surface.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis of osteonecrosis.


Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Humeral head osteonecrosis is caused by an interruption in blood supply to the humeral
head. This results in cell death, bone resorption and remodeling, and subchondral bone
collapse that may lead to joint incongruity and degenerative changes.14
A standard series of shoulder radiographs should be obtained. Pathologic changes to the
humeral head often are best appreciated on an AP view with the humerus in neutral
rotation. Radiographic findings may not be observed during the early phases of the
disease. As the disease progresses, resorption of subchondral bone may be observed as
osteolytic lesions, with the most common initial site being the superior middle portion of
the humeral head. Subchondral collapse may subsequently develop and manifests as a
crescent sign on plain radiographs. Finally, the articular surface may collapse with
resultant glenohumeral arthritis.
As with osteonecrosis of other joints, MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the
diagnosis of humeral head osteonecrosis. Classic findings of bony edema, subchondral
sclerosis and collapse, and flattening of the articular surface can be observed.
Classification Schemes
Staging of humeral head osteonecrosis is important because it directly affects treatment
options and provides insight into expected outcomes.
The Cruess classification system is the most commonly used classification scheme for humeral
head osteonecrosis.

Classification Schemes
Staging and classification of humeral head osteonecrosis is important because treatment
options and expected outcomes largely rely on the severity of the disease. Radiographs
commonly are used to stage disease progression, with the most commonly used

classification scheme being the Cruess classification system15 (Resource 8; Figure 6).
This system was designed as a modification of the Ficat and Arlet system that is used to
stage osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
Stage I is characterized by no radiographic evidence of disease.
Stage II is characterized by signs of mottled sclerosis; however, the curvature of the
humeral head remains intact.
Stage III is characterized by the presence of a crescent sign, indicative of subchondral
fracturing.
Stage IV is characterized by progression to collapse of the subchondral bone.
Stage V is characterized by degenerative changes in the glenoid.
Notably, lesion size is not part of the staging system, whereas lesion size is included in
the classification of femoral head osteonecrosis.

Secondary Arthritis: Etiologies Without Classification Schemes
Pathoanatomy and Imaging Findings
Additional etiologies of secondary shoulder arthritis may not have classification systems but
are important to consider, given the potential impact on treatment options and the ability to
identify potential etiologies based on imaging findings.
Secondary etiologies of shoulder arthritis include dislocation arthropathy, postcapsulorrhaphy
arthropathy, inflammatory arthropathy, chondrolysis, and posttraumatic arthritis.
Dislocation and Postcapsulorrhaphy Arthropathy
Glenohumeral arthritis may result from a single dislocation event.
Radiographic findings typically are similar to those observed in patients with primary
glenohumeral osteoarthritis.
Postcapsulorrhaphy arthropathy results from overtightening of soft-tissue structures during
stabilization procedures for recurrent dislocations.
Dislocation Arthropathy

Dislocation Arthropathy
Dislocation arthropathy is characterized by degenerative changes of the glenohumeral
joint with a history of at least a single dislocation event, with or without surgical
management for instability16 (Resource 9). Radiographs should be obtained for all
patients. CT scans may help further characterize glenoid bone stock and glenoid version
abnormalities. Imaging findings typically include classic findings of joint space narrowing,
large osteophytes, subchondral cysts, subchondral sclerosis, and posterior glenoid wear.
The Samilson-Prieto classification system was proposed for patients with a history of a
single dislocation event. MRI may be helpful in patients with minimal to moderate

arthropathy to identify other potential etiologies that may be contributing to symptoms,

Postcapsulorrhaphy Arthropathy

Postcapsulorrhaphy Arthropathy
Postcapsulorrhaphy arthropathy results from excessive tightening of soft-tissue
structures during stabilization procedures used to manage recurrent dislocations or a
nonanatomic repair (eg, Magnuson-Stack, Putti-Platt, and Bristow procedures). This
results in an asymmetric force of the humeral head on the glenoid. Depending on the
direction of force of the humeral head, this will result in an uneven wear pattern of the
glenoid. Overtightening of anterior soft-tissue structures leads to external rotation
deficits, which may result in posterior glenoid erosion and posterior humeral head
subluxation. The opposite may result from overtightening the posterior soft-tissue
structures. Radiographs often demonstrate these specific findings. In addition, the
presence of orthopaedic implants (eg, staples, screws, metallic anchors) may be
identifiable on radiographs, which may aid in identifying prior procedures performed.
Inflammatory Arthropathy
Radiographic findings commonly observed in patients with rheumatoid arthropathy include
marginal erosions of the humeral head, decreased AHI, and central glenoid wear with
medialization of the humeral head. Dissimilar from osteoarthritis, a paucity of osteophytes
typically is observed in patients with rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthropathy.
Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition (CPPD) disease may result in calcific deposits in
the articular cartilage, termed chondrocalcinosis.
Autoimmune disorders may result in inflammatory arthropathy of the shoulder, with common
disease processes including rheumatoid arthritis, CPPD disease, and gout.
Rheumatoid Arthritis


Rheumatoid Arthritis
Of the inflammatory arthropathies, rheumatoid arthritis is associated with the most
specific and well-defined radiographic findings17 (Resource 10).The earliest radiographic
findings include osteopenia of the humeral head or the glenoid. As the disease
progresses, marginal erosions and cysts develop at the inferior margin of the humeral
head and the glenoid. Erosions may then progress to involve larger portions of the
humeral head, eventually leading to bone loss and flattening of the humeral head. The
glenoid tends to erode centrally, with medialization of the humeral head. Superior
migration of the humeral head with decreases in the AHI may then occur as the rotator
cuff deteriorates. End-stage degenerative changes involve articular destruction with
extensive erosions and bone loss and may involve pseudoarticulation between the
humeral head and the acromion process. Some of the typical radiographic findings
observed in patients with primary osteoarthritis, such as osteophytes and subchondral
sclerosis, are not observed in patients with rheumatoid arthropathy. MRI may be useful
in identifying soft-tissue pathology, particularly joint effusions, synovial inflammation,
pannus formation, capsular distention, and rotator cuff tears. CT may be necessary for
characterization of glenoid morphology and glenoid bone loss, both of which are
important for surgical planning.
CPPD Disease and Gout

CPPD Disease and Gout
Radiographic findings in patients with CPPD disease and gout are not as common and
not as well defined as those in patients with inflammatory arthropathy. CPPD disease
may be associated with radiographic findings of calcific deposits in the articular cartilage,
termed chondrocalcinosis. Gout typically is not associated with any radiographic
findings. Repeated gout flares may eventually result in osteopenia and erosions.
Chondrolysis

Typically observed within months after shoulder arthroscopy
Involves rapid degenerative changes of the articular cartilage
Radiographic findings may be limited early in the disease course, and MRI may be required for
diagnosis.

Chondrolysis
Chondrolysis is joint degeneration and dissolution of articular cartilage. It commonly is
reported after arthroscopy, and has been termed post-arthroscopic glenohumeral
chondrolysis18 (Resource 11). Although the exact pathophysiology remains unknown,
the cause likely is multifactorial and has been associated with radiofrequency ablation,
continuous postoperative intra-articular anesthetic infusions, bioabsorbable suture
anchors, and contrast. These factors may result in rapid degenerative changes as early
as months after an arthroscopic procedure.
A standard shoulder series should initially be obtained if concerns for chondrolysis exist.
Radiographic findings typically include joint space narrowing, periarticular bone erosion,
and subchondral cysts and notably lack osteophytes. If the diagnosis remains
questionable, MRIs can be obtained, which may show a diffuse loss of articular cartilage
on the glenoid and the humeral head. In addition, cortical irregularities and patchy areas
with signal intensity in the subchondral marrow consistent with subchondral sclerosis
may be present.
